tweets: They cut a 20-foot three-faced god straight out of a basalt cliff on an island near Mumbai — then colonial soldiers used him for target practice. He's still standing.

This is the Trimurti Sadashiva, carved around the 6th century inside Elephanta's Great Cave. One bust, three faces: a fierce destroyer, a calm preserver, a serene creator — Shiva as the whole cosmos in stone.

Nothing here was built — it was subtracted. Sculptors hollowed an entire temple straight out of solid basalt rock, cutting corridors, pillars and shrines from one hillside, the same technique later used at Ellora's Kailasa temple.

Elephanta isn't even its original name. Portuguese sailors landed in the early 1500s, found a giant stone elephant near the shore, and renamed the island after it. That statue toppled, was rebuilt, and now stands in a Mumbai garden.

Portuguese troops later used some carvings for shooting practice — the scars are still visible. Yet the Trimurti endured, and in 1987 UNESCO named these caves a World Heritage Site. 1,500 years of gazing out to sea. 🗿 Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
